claim_verdicts.evidence: Scoped re-review: only claims 1, 2 and 17 were re-examined; verdicts for claims 3-16 carry over unchanged from the 2026-09-07T16:45+07:00 review. Claim 1 reworded. GC fundamentals: roots include "local variables on a thread's stack, CPU registers"; 'Stack roots': "JIT optimizations can lengthen or shorten regions of code within which stack variables are reported" — the docs leave per-slot placement open, as the claim now says. stackalloc.md: "A stack-allocated memory block created during the method execution is automatically discarded when that method returns."

Scoped re-review of the reworded claim. Ran nested calls A→B→C on SDK 10.0.300 (Release): output "enter A / enter B / enter C / leave C / leave B / leave A" — the call entered last returns first. Docs: choosing-between-class-and-struct.md "value types are allocated either on the stack … and deallocated when the stack unwinds"; stackalloc.md "You can't explicitly free the memory allocated by stackalloc"; profiling doc: "the reverse of how the frames were pushed onto the stack: leaf (last-pushed) frame first".

GC fundamentals, 'Memory allocation': "All reference types are allocated on the managed heap." struct.md: "Class types have *reference semantics*. That is, a variable of a class type contains a reference to an instance of the type, not the instance itself." .NET 10 caveat checked: whats-new/dotnet-10/runtime.md stack-allocates only boxes, small arrays, delegates and objects held by local struct fields — none of those shapes appears in StackHeap.cs, so the claim stands as written for the pinned version.

GC fundamentals, 'Memory release': the GC "create[s] a graph that contains all the objects that are reachable from the roots. Objects that aren't in the graph are unreachable from the application's roots. The garbage collector considers unreachable objects garbage and releases the memory allocated for them." Only unreachable objects are released, so an object still reached by a root survives the call that created it.

reference-types.md: "Variables of reference types store references to their data (objects)… With reference types, two variables can reference the same object. Therefore, operations on one variable can affect the object referenced by the other variable." Execution today at stage-0 (SDK 10.0.300): `dotnet run --project samples/DonHang.Samples -- stack-heap` → "first.TotalVnd is now 0".

value-types.md: "A variable of a value type contains an instance of the type… you copy variable values. In the case of value-type variables, you copy the corresponding type instances… operations on a value-type variable affect only that instance of the value type, stored in the variable." Execution today printed "oneAmount.AmountVnd is still 1250000".

GC fundamentals, 'Memory release': "The garbage collector's optimizing engine determines the best time to perform a collection based on the allocations being made" and unreachable objects are released "When the garbage collector performs a collection". Scoping checked against the source: StackHeap.cs at stage-0 contains no `GC.` call, so no line in the lesson's code triggers or forces a collection.

GC fundamentals: "developers working with managed code don't have to write code to perform memory management tasks" and 'Benefits': "Frees developers from having to manually release memory." Dispose pattern guidance: "Managed memory (memory allocated using the C# operator new) does not need to be explicitly released. It is released automatically by the garbage collector (GC)."

reference-types.md: "Use the following keywords to declare reference types:" — the list begins with `class`. value-types.md: "A value type can be one of the following kinds: A structure type, which encapsulates data and related functionality." Neither page is version-gated, so it holds for C# 14. Source check: stage-0 has `private sealed class Order { public int TotalVnd; }` and `private struct Money { public int AmountVnd; }` — one int each, nothing else.

Ran `dotnet run --project samples/DonHang.Samples -- stack-heap` in examples/don-hang on 2026-09-07 (SDK 10.0.300). Full output: "first.TotalVnd is now 0" / "oneAmount.AmountVnd is still 1250000" / "both locals disappear when Run returns; the Order does not". The prose numbers in section 5 match this run exactly.

integral-numeric-types.md, 'Integer literals': "The preceding example also shows the use of `_` as a *digit separator*. You can use the digit separator with all kinds of numeric literals." The run confirms the value stored from `1_250_000` prints as 1250000.

GC fundamentals: "Each root either refers to an object on the managed heap or is set to null"; unreachable objects are released only "When the garbage collector performs a collection", whose timing "the garbage collector's optimizing engine determines". Nulling the variable removes one root reference; the memory returns at a later collection, not at that line.

Ran the lesson's own edit on SDK 10.0.300: with `second = new Order { TotalVnd = 7 };` added after the first print, the program printed "misconception-3: first=0 second=7" — first still reaches the original (now zeroed) object and the totals no longer match, as the bullet says. Matches reference-types.md: assignment replaces only the reference held by the assigned variable.

Ran the Try-it variant on SDK 10.0.300 (same code, `private sealed class Money` in place of `private struct Money`): it compiles with no error or warning and prints "first.TotalVnd is now 0" and "oneAmount.AmountVnd is still 0" — both lines report 0, as section 7 promises.
claim_verdicts.source: scratch program on .NET 10.0.300 reproducing StackHeap.cs with Money as a sealed class

claim_verdicts.evidence: Program.cs in the sample project contains `["stack-heap"] = Sync(StackHeap.Run),` and its usage line prints "usage: dotnet run --project samples/DonHang.Samples -- <sample>". The command in section 7 ran successfully and produced this lesson's three lines.

Glossary, 'runtime': "In general, the execution environment for a managed program. The OS is part of the runtime environment but is not part of the .NET runtime" (CLR listed as an example). GC ownership: "In the common language runtime (CLR), the garbage collector (GC) serves as an automatic memory manager" and "Automatic memory management is one of the services that the Common Language Runtime provides".

First half verbatim: sealed.md "When you apply the `sealed` modifier to a class, it prevents other classes from inheriting from that class." Second half is undocumented: sealed.md never mentions allocation; .NET 10 runtime.md ties stack allocation to escape analysis, not to modifiers, yet also says lost devirtualization blocks "inlining and stack allocation" — so a flat "no effect" overstates the docs. Probe on SDK 10.0.300 Release: identical sealed and non-sealed classes each allocated 2,400,000 heap bytes per 100,000 instances.
claim_verdicts.suggested_text: In C# 14, the sealed modifier on a class only prevents other classes from inheriting from it; it is not what decides where an instance lives — a type declared with class is a reference type and its instances are allocated on the managed heap with or without sealed (measured: identical sealed and non-sealed classes allocate the same heap bytes on .NET 10).

issues.text: Claim 17 in .meta.json ends with an absolute the documentation does not state: "it has no effect on where instances of that class are allocated". sealed.md says nothing about allocation, and whats-new/dotnet-10/runtime.md ties stack allocation to escape analysis while noting that lost devirtualization blocks "inlining and stack allocation" — so a blanket "no effect" is broader than any pinned-version source. The lesson sentence itself is fine at the level the lesson works at (class instance on the heap vs struct value in the slot).
issues.fix: Reword claim 17 to the suggested_text of its verdict: sealed only prevents inheritance and is not what decides where an instance lives, since a type declared with class is a reference type and its instances go on the managed heap either way. Leave the Try-it sentence in the lesson unchanged.
issues.quote: it has no effect on where instances of that class are allocated

beyond_scope: Numeric digit separators (section 5, one clause; quiz q5 option e and its explanation) — not an outline item, but forced by the quoted code writing `1_250_000` while the prose and the program output say 1250000. Kept to one clause, so no issue is raised.

issues.text: `sealed` is a word I have never met: it is not in Core concepts and the prose that walks through this block never mentions it. The block is introduced as two types that "differ in the keyword they are declared with", and I see two words on one side (`sealed class`) against one on the other (`struct`), so I stop and wonder whether `sealed` is part of what makes the difference. The answer only arrives two sections later, in a parenthesis inside Try it step 2, and quiz q6 offers `sealed` as a cause.
issues.fix: In section 5, extend the sentence after the first code block: "`Order` is declared with `class` and `Money` with `struct`; `sealed` is there for another reason and has nothing to do with where the object lives." — the same clause already used in Try it step 2.
issues.quote: Each of the two holds a single `int` and nothing else, so that keyword is the only difference that matters below.

issues.text: One sentence earlier I was told each of the four variables has its own slot in the frame and that the frame is on the stack; this sentence says nobody promises where a slot is put, without naming any other place it could be. I re-read it before deciding it means "the arrangement inside the frame does not matter here". The title asks where variables live, so a sentence that refuses to say is the wrong place to be vague.
issues.fix: Make the clause say only what it takes away, e.g. "How the .NET runtime arranges the slots inside the frame is its own business; what matters here is that the slots live and die with the frame."
issues.quote: Exactly where the .NET runtime puts each slot is its own business; what matters here is that the slots live and die with the frame.

issues.text: The gloss explains one thing I do not know with another I do not know: "execution environment". I can still follow the garbage collector bullet, because the rest of the sentence says exactly what it does; but ".NET runtime" comes back in section 4 ("Exactly where the .NET runtime puts each slot") and in a quiz option ("kept by the runtime"), and all I have is a vague idea of it.
issues.fix: Replace the parenthesis with a plainer gloss of the same length, e.g. "(the part of .NET that runs your program)".
issues.quote: the part of the .NET runtime (the execution environment .NET gives your program while it runs)

issues.text: The lesson before this one told me a system tool lists the processes alive with their ids; it never said such a tool also shows how much memory a process uses, so I have to take that on faith here. Quiz q4 asks me to "watch the memory a system tool reports for your process" as well. I also had to re-read the sentence because of the two dashes in the middle of it.
issues.fix: Add the missing half-step: "the same kind of tool that listed processes and their ids, which also reports how much memory each one is using", and split the sentence at the first dash.
issues.quote: the memory a system tool reports for your process — the same kind of tool that listed processes and their ids — does not fall at the line you expected

issues.text: This one paragraph carries the frame, the four variables, the slots, the runtime's freedom, the teardown and the reverse order. "needs no decision to release" is abstract at that point, because nothing in the lesson has had to be released yet — the garbage collector only appears two paragraphs later. I read the paragraph twice before it held together.
issues.fix: Split the paragraph after "the slots live and die with the frame." and replace "needs no decision to release" with "nobody has to give back".
issues.quote: That is why this memory needs no decision to release: it is taken back with the call that owns it — the frame added last is the first one to go.

issues.text: Options a and d are almost word for word a sentence I had just read in section 5, so I can pick them by matching wording against the text rather than by working out what happens in the run; the two wrong options echo nothing from the lesson, which makes the matching easier still.
issues.fix: Reword q5 options a and d so they do not repeat section 5's sentence: say what each printed line shows and how many objects exist, without reusing "writing through `second` is writing through `first`" and "two slots in the frame that both reach it".
issues.quote: `new Order` puts one object on the heap, and `first` and `second` are two slots in the frame that both reach it, so writing through `second` is writing through `first`
